\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The two invariants}

Throughout, $G$ is a finite group acting on a finite set $X$, and we write
\[
  X^g=\{x\in X: g\cdot x=x\},\qquad \operatorname{fix}(g)=|X^g|\in\{0,1,\dots,|X|\}.
\]

\begin{definition}[Fixed-point $q$-series]
$\displaystyle \Phi_{G,X}(q)=\sum_{g\in G}q^{\,|X^g|}\in\mathbb{Q}[q]$.
\end{definition}

Equivalently $\Phi_{G,X}$ is the generating polynomial of the \emph{fixed-point multiset}
$\mathcal{M}_{G,X}=\{\!\{\,|X^g|:g\in G\,\}\!\}$, a multiset of $|G|$ integers in $[0,|X|]$. Its
coefficient at $q^{v}$ is the \emph{fibre cardinality}
$F_{G,X}(v)=\#\{g\in G:|X^g|=v\}$.

\begin{definition}[Fixed-point density]
$\displaystyle \rho_{G,X}(v)=F_{G,X}(v)/|G|\in\mathbb{Q}_{\ge0}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Orbit counts]
Let $G$ act on $X^{\times n}$ diagonally. Put
$N_{G,X}(n)=\bigl|X^{\times n}/G\bigr|$ and
$N_{G,X}(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}N_{G,X}(n)t^{n}$.
\end{definition}

\subsection{Summary of results}

\begin{theoremletter}[Burnside for tuples; moment identity]\label{thmA}
For every $n\ge0$,
\[
  |G|\cdot N_{G,X}(n)=\sum_{g\in G}|X^g|^{\,n},
  \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
  N_{G,X}(n)=\sum_{v=0}^{|X|}\rho_{G,X}(v)\,v^{\,n}.
\]
\end{theoremletter}

\begin{theoremletter}[Molien-type closed form]\label{thmB}
As formal power series, $|G|\cdot N_{G,X}(t)=\sum_{g\in G}\bigl(1-|X^g|t\bigr)^{-1}$, and
consequently $\prod_{g\in G}(1-|X^g|t)\cdot |G|\cdot N_{G,X}(t)$ is a polynomial.
\end{theoremletter}

\begin{theoremletter}[Rigidity and dichotomy]\label{thmC}
Let $G$ act on $X$ and $H$ on $Y$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\Phi_{G,X}=\Phi_{H,Y}$ then $N_{G,X}(n)=N_{H,Y}(n)$ for all $n$.
\item If $N_{G,X}(n)=N_{H,Y}(n)$ for all $n\le\max(|X|,|Y|)$, then $\rho_{G,X}=\rho_{H,Y}$.
\item If moreover $|G|=|H|$, then either $\Phi_{G,X}=\Phi_{H,Y}$, or there is some
$n\le\max(|X|,|Y|)$ with $N_{G,X}(n)\ne N_{H,Y}(n)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theoremletter}

\begin{theoremletter}[Linear reconstruction]\label{thmD}
Let $N=|X|$ and let $M^{(N)}$ be the $(N{+}1)\times(N{+}1)$ matrix with
$M^{(N)}_{n,j}=j^{\,n}$. Then $M^{(N)}$ is invertible; write $C^{(N)}=(M^{(N)})^{-1}$. For every
$v\le N$,
\[
  \rho_{G,X}(v)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}C^{(N)}_{v,n}\cdot N_{G,X}(n),
\]
where $C^{(N)}$ depends only on $N$ --- not on $G$, on the action, or on $|G|$.
\end{theoremletter}

\begin{theoremletter}[Peeling recursion]\label{thmE}
For $1\le m\le|X|$,
\[
  \rho_{G,X}(m)=\lim_{n\to\infty}
  \frac{N_{G,X}(n)-\sum_{v=m+1}^{|X|}\rho_{G,X}(v)\,v^{\,n}}{m^{\,n}},
\]
and $\rho_{G,X}(0)=1-\sum_{v=1}^{|X|}\rho_{G,X}(v)$. The top step $m=|X|$ reads
$N_{G,X}(n)/|X|^{\,n}\to|K|/|G|$, where $K$ is the kernel of the action.
\end{theoremletter}

\begin{theoremletter}[Quantitative peeling; exact termination]\label{thmF}
With $P_m(n)$ the quantity inside the limit of Theorem~\ref{thmE},
$\bigl|P_m(n)-\rho_{G,X}(m)\bigr|\le\bigl(\tfrac{m-1}{m}\bigr)^{n}$, and whenever
$\bigl(\tfrac{m-1}{m}\bigr)^{n}\cdot2|G|<1$ --- which happens for some $n$ ---
$F_{G,X}(m)=\round\bigl(|G|\cdot P_m(n)\bigr)$ exactly.
\end{theoremletter}

\begin{theoremletter}[Sharpness and blind spots]\label{thmG}
\begin{enumerate}
\item The trivial actions of the groups of order $1$ and $2$ on a two-element set have identical
orbit counts and densities, but $q$-series $q^{2}$ and $2q^{2}$.
\item The signed weight $(1,-3,3,-1)$ on nodes $\{0,1,2,3\}$ kills the power sums for
$n=0,1,2$ but not for $n=3$.
\item The regular actions of $\Zmod4$ and $\Zmod2\times\Zmod2$ have equal $q$-series and equal
orbit counts in every degree, yet the groups are not isomorphic.
\item If $G=H$, then $N_{G,X}(n)=N_{G,Y}(n)$ for all $n\le\max(|X|,|Y|)$ if and only if
$\mathcal{M}_{G,X}=\mathcal{M}_{G,Y}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theoremletter}

\subsection{Context}
Theorem~\ref{thmB} is the combinatorial analogue of Molien's series for invariants of a linear
group, with fixed-point counts in place of eigenvalue data. Theorem~\ref{thmC} is best read as a
\emph{moment problem}: the fixed-point density is a probability measure on the finite grid
$\{0,\dots,|X|\}$, and a measure supported on $k$ known nodes is determined by its first $k$
moments. This is why the proof is interpolation rather than group theory, and why the correct
converse invariant is $\rho$ rather than $\Phi$: the normalisation by $|G|$ destroys exactly one
degree of freedom, namely scale.

\section{The algebraic core: finite determinacy of weighted power sums}

\begin{lemma}[Finite determinacy]\label{lem:determinacy}
Let $S$ be a finite index set of size $k$, let $\mathrm{val}:S\to\mathbb{Q}$ be injective, and
let $w:S\to\mathbb{Q}$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in S}w(i)\,\mathrm{val}(i)^{n}=0$ for
$n=0,1,\dots,k-1$. Then $w\equiv0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Fix $u\in S$ and let $L_u(T)=\prod_{i\ne u}\frac{T-\mathrm{val}(i)}{\mathrm{val}(u)-\mathrm{val}(i)}$
be the Lagrange basis polynomial at $u$; it is well defined by injectivity, has degree $k-1$,
and satisfies $L_u(\mathrm{val}(u))=1$ and $L_u(\mathrm{val}(i))=0$ for $i\ne u$. Hence
$w(u)=\sum_{i\in S}w(i)L_u(\mathrm{val}(i))$. Writing $L_u(T)=\sum_{n<k}c_nT^{n}$ and
exchanging the finite sums, $w(u)=\sum_{n<k}c_n\sum_{i}w(i)\mathrm{val}(i)^{n}=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:determinacy-eq}
If $w,w':S\to\mathbb{Q}$ have equal weighted power sums for all $n<|S|$, then $w=w'$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[Sharpness of the exponent range]\label{rem:sharp}
Lemma~\ref{lem:determinacy} fails if only $n<k-1$ is assumed. On $\{0,1,2,3\}$ take
$w=(1,-3,3,-1)$: then $\sum_v w(v)=0$, $\sum_v w(v)v=0$, $\sum_v w(v)v^{2}=0$, while
$\sum_v w(v)v^{3}=-6\ne0$. In general the alternating binomial vector
$\bigl((-1)^{j}\binom{k-1}{j}\bigr)_j$ is the $(k-1)$-st finite-difference functional and
annihilates every polynomial of degree $<k-1$.
\end{remark}

\section{Burnside's lemma as a moment identity}

\begin{theorem}[Theorem~\ref{thmA}]\label{thm:burnside}
For all $n\ge0$, $|G|\cdot N_{G,X}(n)=\sum_{g\in G}|X^g|^{\,n}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Burnside's lemma for a finite action on $Z$ reads $|G|\cdot|Z/G|=\sum_g|Z^g|$. Apply it to
$Z=X^{\times n}$ with the diagonal action; a tuple is fixed by $g$ iff every entry is, so
$(X^{\times n})^{g}=(X^{g})^{\times n}$ has $|X^g|^{n}$ elements.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Moment form]\label{cor:moment}
Grouping group elements by fixed-point count and dividing by $|G|$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:moment}
  N_{G,X}(n)=\sum_{v=0}^{|X|}\rho_{G,X}(v)\,v^{\,n}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[$\rho$ is a probability distribution]\label{cor:prob}
Taking $n=0$ gives $N_{G,X}(0)=1$ and $\sum_{v=0}^{|X|}\rho_{G,X}(v)=1$. Since the densities are
nonnegative, every partial sum satisfies $\sum_{v<m}\rho_{G,X}(v)\le1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Theorem~\ref{thmB}]\label{thm:molien}
In $\mathbb{Q}[[t]]$, $|G|\cdot N_{G,X}(t)=\sum_{g\in G}\bigl(1-|X^g|t\bigr)^{-1}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For a scalar $a$, $(1-at)\sum_{n\ge0}a^{n}t^{n}=1$, so $\sum_n a^n t^n$ inverts $1-at$.
Comparing coefficients of $t^{n}$ reduces the claim to Theorem~\ref{thm:burnside}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Rationality]\label{cor:rational}
$\bigl(\prod_{g}(1-|X^g|t)\bigr)\cdot|G|\cdot N_{G,X}(t)=\sum_{g}\prod_{h\ne g}(1-|X^h|t)$,
a polynomial of degree $\le|G|-1$. Hence $N_{G,X}$ is rational with poles among the reciprocals
$1/v$ of the nonzero fixed-point counts.
\end{corollary}

\section{Rigidity: two directions and a dichotomy}

Let $G$ act on $X$ and $H$ on $Y$, and put $S=\{0,1,\dots,\max(|X|,|Y|)\}$, so
$|S|=\max(|X|,|Y|)+1$; both densities are supported in $S$.

\begin{theorem}[Forward rigidity]\label{thm:forward}
If $\rho_{G,X}=\rho_{H,Y}$ then $N_{G,X}(n)=N_{H,Y}(n)$ for all $n$. In particular
$\Phi_{G,X}=\Phi_{H,Y}$ implies $N_{G,X}=N_{H,Y}$, with no hypothesis on group orders.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from \eqref{eq:moment}. For the second claim, equality of $q$-series gives equality of
the fixed-point multisets, hence $|G|=|H|$ (both multisets have those cardinalities), hence
equal fibre cardinalities and equal densities.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Converse rigidity, finite]\label{thm:converse}
If $N_{G,X}(n)=N_{H,Y}(n)$ for all $n\le\max(|X|,|Y|)$, then $\rho_{G,X}=\rho_{H,Y}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Outside $S$ both densities vanish. On $S$ the hypothesis and \eqref{eq:moment} give
$\sum_{v\in S}\rho_{G,X}(v)v^{n}=\sum_{v\in S}\rho_{H,Y}(v)v^{n}$ for all $n<|S|$; the nodes are
distinct rationals, so Corollary~\ref{cor:determinacy-eq} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Rigidity, iff form; dichotomy]\label{thm:dichotomy}
Suppose $|G|=|H|$. Then $\Phi_{G,X}=\Phi_{H,Y}$ if and only if $N_{G,X}(n)=N_{H,Y}(n)$ for all
$n$. Consequently exactly one of the following holds: either $\Phi_{G,X}=\Phi_{H,Y}$, or there
exists $n\le\max(|X|,|Y|)$ with $N_{G,X}(n)\ne N_{H,Y}(n)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
One direction is Theorem~\ref{thm:forward}. Conversely Theorem~\ref{thm:converse} gives
$\rho_{G,X}=\rho_{H,Y}$; multiplying by the common order $|G|=|H|$ gives equality of fibre
cardinalities, i.e.\ of $q$-series. The dichotomy is the resulting case split.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Graded form]\label{thm:graded}
Let $(X_m)_{m\ge0}$ be finite $G$-sets and $(Y_m)_{m\ge0}$ finite $H$-sets with $|G|=|H|$. Then
$\Phi_{G,X_m}=\Phi_{H,Y_m}$ for all $m$ if and only if $N_{G,X_m}(n)=N_{H,Y_m}(n)$ for all
$m,n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Kernel proportion and detection of triviality]\label{thm:kernel}
Let $K=\{g:g\cdot x=x\ \forall x\}$, so $|K|=F_{G,X}(|X|)$. Then
\begin{enumerate}
\item $|K|\,|X|^{n}\le|G|\,N_{G,X}(n)\le|K|\,|X|^{n}+(|G|-|K|)(|X|-1)^{n}$;
\item equal orbit counts up to $\max(|X|,|Y|)$ with $|X|=|Y|$ force $|K_G|/|G|=|K_H|/|H|$;
\item $N_{G,X}(n)=|X|^{n}$ for all $n$ if and only if the action is trivial, and the single
value $n=1$ already decides this.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) Split the Burnside sum into kernel elements (contributing $|X|^{n}$ each) and the rest
(contributing at most $(|X|-1)^{n}$ each). (2) is Theorem~\ref{thm:converse} at $v=|X|$.
(3) Substituting $N_{G,X}(1)=|X|$ into the upper bound of (1) gives
$|G||X|\le|G||X|-(|G|-|K|)$, so $|K|=|G|$.
\end{proof}

\section{Effective reconstruction I: the universal linear formula}

\begin{definition}[Moment matrix]
For $N\ge0$ let $M^{(N)}_{n,j}=j^{\,n}$, $0\le n,j\le N$, with rows indexed by exponents and
columns by nodes.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:vandermonde}
$M^{(N)}$ is the transpose of the Vandermonde matrix of the nodes $0,1,\dots,N$, with
$\det M^{(N)}=\prod_{0\le i<j\le N}(j-i)\ne0$. Hence $M^{(N)}$ is invertible.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}
$C^{(N)}=\bigl(M^{(N)}\bigr)^{-1}$, with entries $C^{(N)}_{v,n}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Inversion of the moment map]\label{lem:inversion}
For any $w\in\mathbb{Q}^{N+1}$ and any $v\le N$,
$w_v=\sum_{n=0}^{N}C^{(N)}_{v,n}\bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{N}w_j\,j^{\,n}\bigr)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The inner sum is the $n$-th coordinate of $M^{(N)}w$; applying the inverse recovers $w$. No
positivity or normalisation is used.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Theorem~\ref{thmD}]\label{thm:recon}
Let $N=|X|$. For every $v\le N$,
$\rho_{G,X}(v)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}C^{(N)}_{v,n}\cdot N_{G,X}(n)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:inversion} with $w_j=\rho_{G,X}(j)$; by \eqref{eq:moment} the inner power
sum is $N_{G,X}(n)$.
\end{proof}

Three features deserve emphasis. \emph{Universality}: $C^{(N)}$ depends on $N$ alone --- not on
$G$, on the action, or even on $|G|$. \emph{Finiteness}: only $N+1$ orbit counts enter, matching
Theorem~\ref{thm:converse} and, by Remark~\ref{rem:sharp}, unimprovable in general.
\emph{A second proof of rigidity}: if the counts agree in degrees $0,\dots,N$, the two densities
are the same linear functional of the same inputs. This also yields a separation criterion: if
$\rho_{G,X}(v)\ne\rho_{H,Y}(v)$ for some $v$, the counts already differ at some $n\le|X|$.

\begin{example}[$N=2$]\label{ex:N2}
On $\{0,1,2\}$,
\[
  M^{(2)}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\0&1&2\\0&1&4\end{pmatrix},\qquad
  C^{(2)}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-\tfrac32&\tfrac12\\[2pt]0&2&-1\\[2pt]0&-\tfrac12&\tfrac12\end{pmatrix}.
\]
So for any action on a two-element set $\rho(2)=\tfrac12(N_2-N_1)$, $\rho(1)=2N_1-N_2$, and
$\rho(0)=N_0-\tfrac32N_1+\tfrac12N_2$. For $\Sym(\{0,1\})$ acting naturally,
$(N_0,N_1,N_2)=(1,1,2)$ and $\rho=(\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12)$.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[Conditioning]
Vandermonde matrices are notoriously ill-conditioned, so over $\mathbb{R}$ this inversion is
numerically fatal for even moderate $N$; over $\mathbb{Q}$ it is exact and harmless. This is the
practical motivation for the second method.
\end{remark}

\section{Effective reconstruction II: the peeling recursion}

\begin{lemma}[Peeling step]\label{lem:peel}
Let $m\ge1$ and $w:\{0,\dots,m\}\to\mathbb{R}$. Then
$\lim_{n\to\infty}m^{-n}\sum_{v\le m}w(v)v^{n}=w(m)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$m^{-n}\sum_{v\le m}w(v)v^{n}=w(m)+\sum_{v<m}w(v)(v/m)^{n}$, and each ratio $v/m$ lies in
$[0,1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Peeled estimate]
For $1\le m\le|X|$,
$P_m(n)=m^{-n}\bigl(N_{G,X}(n)-\sum_{v=m+1}^{|X|}\rho_{G,X}(v)v^{n}\bigr)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Splitting the moment]\label{lem:split}
For $m\le|X|$, $N_{G,X}(n)-\sum_{v>m}\rho_{G,X}(v)v^{n}=\sum_{v\le m}\rho_{G,X}(v)v^{n}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Theorem~\ref{thmE}]\label{thm:peel}
For $1\le m\le|X|$, $\rho_{G,X}(m)=\lim_{n\to\infty}P_m(n)$, and
$\rho_{G,X}(0)=1-\sum_{v=1}^{|X|}\rho_{G,X}(v)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Lemma~\ref{lem:split} with Lemma~\ref{lem:peel} applied to $w=\rho_{G,X}$; the last
statement is Corollary~\ref{cor:prob}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Top step equals kernel asymptotics]\label{cor:top}
For $|X|\ge1$, $N_{G,X}(n)/|X|^{n}\to\rho_{G,X}(|X|)=|K|/|G|$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Error bound]\label{thm:error}
For $1\le m\le|X|$ and every $n$,
$0\le P_m(n)-\rho_{G,X}(m)\le\bigl(\tfrac{m-1}{m}\bigr)^{n}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:split}, $P_m(n)-\rho_{G,X}(m)=\sum_{v<m}\rho_{G,X}(v)(v/m)^{n}\ge0$. Each
$v<m$ satisfies $v\le m-1$, so each factor is at most $((m-1)/m)^{n}$, and the total mass below
$m$ is at most $1$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:prob}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact termination]\label{thm:exact}
Let $1\le m\le|X|$ and suppose $\bigl(\tfrac{m-1}{m}\bigr)^{n}\cdot2|G|<1$. Then
$F_{G,X}(m)=\round\bigl(|G|\cdot P_m(n)\bigr)$. Such an $n$ always exists.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Multiplying Theorem~\ref{thm:error} by $|G|$ and using $|G|\rho_{G,X}(m)=F_{G,X}(m)$ gives
$\bigl||G|P_m(n)-F_{G,X}(m)\bigr|<\tfrac12$, and an integer within distance $<\tfrac12$ of a
rational is its nearest integer. Existence follows from $(m-1)/m<1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The condition reads $n\log\frac{m}{m-1}>\log(2|G|)$, i.e.\ roughly $n>m\log(2|G|)$, so peeling
uses $O(|X|\log|G|)$ orbit counts --- more than the provably minimal $|X|+1$ of
Theorem~\ref{thm:recon}, but through numerically stable, positively weighted steps with a
certified error at every stage. For $m=1$ the error term is $0^{n}$ and $n=1$ suffices.
\end{remark}

\section{Sharpness: exactly what is lost}

\begin{theorem}[Normalisation is necessary]\label{thm:norm}
Let $E$ be the trivial group and $C_2$ the group of order $2$, both acting trivially on a
two-element set $B$. Then $N_{E,B}(n)=N_{C_2,B}(n)=2^{n}$ for all $n$ and
$\rho_{E,B}=\rho_{C_2,B}=\delta_2$, but $\Phi_{E,B}(q)=q^{2}\ne2q^{2}=\Phi_{C_2,B}(q)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Under a trivial action every element fixes every point and every orbit is a singleton, so
$N(n)=2^{n}$ and the density is the point mass at $2$; the unnormalised $q$-series records
$|G|$.
\end{proof}

Hence the converse in Theorem~\ref{thmC} cannot be strengthened from densities to $q$-series
without assuming $|G|=|H|$: orbit counts are blind to the group order because Burnside divides
by it.

By Remark~\ref{rem:sharp}, on $k$ nodes there is a nonzero signed weight annihilating the first
$k-1$ power sums, so the exponent range in Theorem~\ref{thm:converse} cannot be shortened at the
level of the underlying linear algebra.

\begin{theorem}[Regular actions]\label{thm:regular}
Let $G$ act on itself by left multiplication. Then $|G^{g}|=|G|$ if $g=1$ and $0$ otherwise, so
$\Phi_{G,G}(q)=q^{|G|}+(|G|-1)$ and $N_{G,G}(n+1)=|G|^{n}$, i.e.\
$N_{G,G}(t)=1+\frac{t}{1-|G|t}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[The exact blind spot]\label{cor:blind}
Two regular actions are indistinguishable by both invariants precisely when the groups have the
same order. In particular $\Zmod4$ and $\Zmod2\times\Zmod2$ acting on themselves have identical
$q$-series $q^{4}+3$ and identical orbit counts $1,1,4,16,64,\dots$, yet are not isomorphic.
\end{corollary}

So Theorem~\ref{thmC} is optimal in the strongest sense: it determines the fixed-point
distribution, and can never be upgraded to determine the group up to isomorphism.

\begin{theorem}[Same-group upgrade]\label{thm:samegroup}
Let one group $G$ act on finite sets $X$ and $Y$. Then
$N_{G,X}(n)=N_{G,Y}(n)$ for all $n\le\max(|X|,|Y|)$ if and only if
$\mathcal{M}_{G,X}=\mathcal{M}_{G,Y}$, if and only if $\Phi_{G,X}=\Phi_{G,Y}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:converse} gives equality of densities; multiplying by the common $|G|$ gives
equality of fibre cardinalities. The converse is Theorem~\ref{thm:forward}.
\end{proof}

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algo}[Vandermonde inversion]
\emph{Input}: $N$, exact orbit counts $N_0,\dots,N_N$, group order $|G|$.
\emph{Output}: densities $\rho(0..N)$ and fibre counts $F(0..N)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Build $M$ with $M_{n,j}=j^{n}$ for $0\le n,j\le N$.
\item Solve $Mx=(N_0,\dots,N_N)^{\mathsf T}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ by exact elimination.
\item Set $\rho(v)=x_v$ and $F(v)=|G|\rho(v)$.
\end{enumerate}
Cost: $O(N^{3})$ exact rational operations (or $O(N^{2})$ with a Vandermonde-specialised
solver); uses exactly $N+1$ orbit counts, the provable minimum.
\end{algo}

\begin{algo}[Peeling with certified rounding]
\emph{Input}: $N$, $|G|$, an oracle for $N_{G,X}(n)$ at arbitrary $n$.
\emph{Output}: fibre counts $F(0..N)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For $m=N$ down to $1$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item choose the least $n$ with $((m-1)/m)^{n}\cdot2|G|<1$ (take $n=1$ if $m=1$);
\item compute $S=\sum_{v>m}\rho(v)v^{n}$ from the already-known values;
\item set $P=(N_n-S)/m^{n}$, $F(m)=\round(|G|P)$, $\rho(m)=F(m)/|G|$.
\end{enumerate}
\item Set $F(0)=|G|-\sum_{v\ge1}F(v)$.
\end{enumerate}
Cost: $O(N)$ oracle calls at exponents $n=O(N\log|G|)$, plus $O(N^{2})$ arithmetic operations on
integers of $O(N^{2}\log|G|)$ bits. Every step is certified by Theorem~\ref{thm:error} and exact
by Theorem~\ref{thm:exact}.
\end{algo}

Both algorithms are exact: no floating point arithmetic is required at any stage.

\section{Applications and interpretation}

\emph{Inverse P\'olya enumeration.} Classical P\'olya theory runs forwards, from a group to a
counting series. Theorems~\ref{thmD}--\ref{thmF} run it backwards: from observed counts of
inequivalent configurations one recovers the complete fixed-point statistics of an unseen
symmetry group, from $|X|+1$ data points, exactly.

\emph{Spectral reading.} By Corollary~\ref{cor:rational} the orbit-counting series is rational
with poles at $1/v$ for each realised fixed-point count $v$ and residues proportional to
$F(v)$. Peeling is residue extraction ordered by pole size, and Corollary~\ref{cor:top} says the
dominant pole $1/|X|$ has residue proportional to the kernel size.

\emph{A discrete moment problem with an exact stopping rule.} The measure here is supported on a
known finite grid \emph{and} has bounded denominator $|G|$. That arithmetic rigidity converts an
asymptotic limit into a finite algorithm. The pattern --- geometric approximation, plus a
denominator bound, plus rounding --- is a general recipe for exactifying limits.

\emph{A resolution statement.} Combining Theorem~\ref{thm:norm} and Corollary~\ref{cor:blind},
the map from a finite $G$-set to its orbit-counting series factors exactly through the density
$\rho$ and nothing finer: it forgets the group order, the group and the action, and remembers
$\rho$ completely.

\section{Discussion and future work}

The instructive point is how the naive conjecture fails. One might guess that orbit counts
determine the fixed-point multiset; Theorem~\ref{thm:norm} shows this is false for a structural
reason. Once the right invariant is identified --- the probability measure $\rho$ --- the problem
becomes a moment problem on a finite grid, and interpolation solves it completely.

Open directions include: (i) realising the sharpness vector of Remark~\ref{rem:sharp} as a
difference of two genuine fixed-point distributions of equal-order groups, a realisation problem
for permutation characters; (ii) proving that for all but a vanishing fraction of pairs of
faithful transitive actions on $k$ points only $O(\log k)$ coefficients are needed to separate
them, exploiting positivity and the transitive normalisation $\sum_g|X^g|=|G|$; (iii) replacing
fixed-point counts by traces of a linear representation, recovering the classical Molien series
and a rigidity statement for eigenvalue distributions; and (iv) stability of the two algorithms
under noisy counts, where Vandermonde inversion amplifies error exponentially while peeling,
with its positive-mass bound, should degrade gracefully.

  "demo": """"
Molien-type rigidity for finite group actions: numerical demonstrations.

Setting
-------
A finite group G acts on a finite set X (here: X = {0, 1, ..., N-1}, and G is given
concretely as a list of permutations of X, i.e. tuples p with p[i] = image of i).

Two invariants are attached to the action:

  * the fixed-point q-series   Phi(q) = sum_{g in G} q^{|X^g|},
    equivalently the fibre counts F(v) = #{g : |X^g| = v},
    equivalently the normalised density rho(v) = F(v)/|G|;

  * the orbit counts           N_n = #( X^n / G )  (diagonal action on n-tuples).

Burnside's lemma on n-tuples gives the moment identity

        |G| * N_n = sum_g |X^g|^n        i.e.       N_n = sum_v rho(v) * v^n,

so the orbit counts are exactly the moments of the fixed-point density.  Everything
below is a consequence.

This script demonstrates, in exact rational arithmetic:

  1. the moment identity (Burnside for tuples) and the Molien rational form;
  2. reconstruction of rho from the first |X|+1 orbit counts by inverting the
     Vandermonde/moment matrix -- with universal coefficients depending only on |X|;
  3. the peeling recursion, its explicit geometric error bound ((m-1)/m)^n, and the
     rounding rule that makes the limit an exact terminating computation;
  4. the sharpness statements: normalisation cannot be removed, the number of
     coefficients cannot be reduced, and the invariants cannot distinguish groups
     (Z/4 versus Z/2 x Z/2 acting regularly).

Self-contained: standard library only.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Perm = Tuple[int, ...]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Basic group / action machinery
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def compose(p: Perm, q: Perm) -> Perm:
    """Composition (p after q): (p*q)[i] = p[q[i]]."""
    return tuple(p[q[i]] for i in range(len(p)))


def generated_group(gens: Sequence[Perm], degree: int) -> List[Perm]:
    """Closure of `gens` under composition, containing the identity."""
    identity: Perm = tuple(range(degree))
    elements: Dict[Perm, None] = {identity: None}
    frontier: List[Perm] = [identity]
    while frontier:
        new_frontier: List[Perm] = []
        for element in frontier:
            for g in gens:
                candidate = compose(g, element)
                if candidate not in elements:
                    elements[candidate] = None
                    new_frontier.append(candidate)
        frontier = new_frontier
    return sorted(elements)


def fix_count(p: Perm) -> int:
    """Number of points fixed by the permutation p."""
    return sum(1 for i, image in enumerate(p) if image == i)


def fibre_counts(group: Sequence[Perm], degree: int) -> List[int]:
    """F(v) = #{g in G : |X^g| = v} for v = 0..degree."""
    counts = [0] * (degree + 1)
    for p in group:
        counts[fix_count(p)] += 1
    return counts


def density(group: Sequence[Perm], degree: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    """rho(v) = F(v) / |G| for v = 0..degree."""
    order = len(group)
    return [Fraction(f, order) for f in fibre_counts(group, degree)]


def q_series_string(group: Sequence[Perm], degree: int) -> str:
    """Human-readable fixed-point q-series Phi(q) = sum_g q^{|X^g|}."""
    counts = fibre_counts(group, degree)
    terms: List[str] = []
    for v in range(degree, -1, -1):
        c = counts[v]
        if c == 0:
            continue
        coeff = "" if (c == 1 and v > 0) else str(c)
        if v == 0:
            terms.append(str(c))
        elif v == 1:
            terms.append(f"{coeff}q")
        else:
            terms.append(f"{coeff}q^{v}")
    return " + ".join(terms) if terms else "0"


def orbit_count_bruteforce(group: Sequence[Perm], degree: int, n: int) -> int:
    """#(X^n / G), computed by explicit orbit enumeration (small n only)."""
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    seen = set()
    orbits = 0
    for tup in product(range(degree), repeat=n):
        if tup in seen:
            continue
        orbits += 1
        for p in group:
            seen.add(tuple(p[x] for x in tup))
    return orbits


def orbit_count_burnside(group: Sequence[Perm], n: int) -> int:
    """#(X^n / G) via Burnside: (1/|G|) sum_g |X^g|^n."""
    total = sum(fix_count(p) ** n for p in group)
    assert total % len(group) == 0
    return total // len(group)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Exact linear algebra over Q: Vandermonde inversion
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def moment_matrix(size: int) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    """M[n][j] = j^n for 0 <= n, j <= size (transpose of the Vandermonde matrix)."""
    return [[Fraction(j) ** n for j in range(size + 1)] for n in range(size + 1)]


def invert_matrix(matrix: List[List[Fraction]]) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    """Exact Gauss-Jordan inversion over the rationals."""
    dim = len(matrix)
    work = [row[:] + [Fraction(1 if i == j else 0) for j in range(dim)]
            for i, row in enumerate(matrix)]
    for col in range(dim):
        pivot = next(r for r in range(col, dim) if work[r][col] != 0)
        work[col], work[pivot] = work[pivot], work[col]
        scale = work[col][col]
        work[col] = [entry / scale for entry in work[col]]
        for r in range(dim):
            if r != col and work[r][col] != 0:
                factor = work[r][col]
                work[r] = [a - factor * b for a, b in zip(work[r], work[col])]
    return [row[dim:] for row in work]


def reconstruction_matrix(size: int) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    """C = M^{-1}: the universal reconstruction coefficients on nodes 0..size."""
    return invert_matrix(moment_matrix(size))


def reconstruct_density(orbit_counts: Sequence[int], size: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    """rho(v) = sum_{n<=size} C[v][n] * N_n, using exactly size+1 orbit counts."""
    coeff = reconstruction_matrix(size)
    return [sum((coeff[v][n] * orbit_counts[n] for n in range(size + 1)), Fraction(0))
            for v in range(size + 1)]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The peeling recursion, with certified rounding
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def peel_estimate(orbit_counts_at_n: Fraction, known_above: Sequence[Fraction],
                  m: int, size: int, n: int) -> Fraction:
    """P_m(n) = (N_n - sum_{v>m} rho(v) v^n) / m^n, with known_above indexed by v."""
    tail = sum((known_above[v] * Fraction(v) ** n for v in range(m + 1, size + 1)),
               Fraction(0))
    return (orbit_counts_at_n - tail) / Fraction(m) ** n


def peel_stopping_time(m: int, group_order: int) -> int:
    """Least n with ((m-1)/m)^n * 2|G| < 1 (n = 1 when m = 1, where the error is 0)."""
    if m == 1:
        return 1
    ratio = Fraction(m - 1, m)
    n = 1
    while ratio ** n * 2 * group_order >= 1:
        n += 1
    return n


def round_half_up(x: Fraction) -> int:
    """Nearest integer to the rational x."""
    from math import floor
    return floor(x + Fraction(1, 2))


def peel_reconstruct(group: Sequence[Perm], size: int) -> Tuple[List[int], List[int]]:
    """
    Reconstruct the fibre counts F(0..size) purely from orbit counts, top down.

    Returns (fibre counts, the exponent n used at each value m).
    Uses only |G| and an oracle for the orbit counts; never inspects the group's
    fixed-point data directly.
    """
    order = len(group)
    rho: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(0)] * (size + 1)
    fibres: List[int] = [0] * (size + 1)
    exponents: List[int] = [0] * (size + 1)
    for m in range(size, 0, -1):
        n = peel_stopping_time(m, order)
        exponents[m] = n
        n_at = Fraction(orbit_count_burnside(group, n))
        estimate = peel_estimate(n_at, rho, m, size, n)
        fibres[m] = round_half_up(Fraction(order) * estimate)
        rho[m] = Fraction(fibres[m], order)
    fibres[0] = order - sum(fibres[1:])
    return fibres, exponents


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Demonstrations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def banner(text: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(text)
    print("=" * 78)


def show_action(name: str, group: Sequence[Perm], degree: int,
                max_n: int = 6, verify_bruteforce_upto: int = 4) -> None:
    banner(f"{name}   (|G| = {len(group)}, |X| = {degree})")

    counts = fibre_counts(group, degree)
    rho = density(group, degree)
    print(f"fixed-point q-series  Phi(q) = {q_series_string(group, degree)}")
    print(f"fibre counts F(v)            = {counts}")
    print(f"density rho(v)               = {[str(r) for r in rho]}")
    print(f"total mass                   = {sum(rho, Fraction(0))}")

    burnside = [orbit_count_burnside(group, n) for n in range(max_n + 1)]
    print(f"orbit counts N_0..N_{max_n}        = {burnside}")

    # 1. Burnside for tuples, checked against brute-force orbit enumeration.
    for n in range(verify_bruteforce_upto + 1):
        brute = orbit_count_bruteforce(group, degree, n)
        assert brute == burnside[n], (n, brute, burnside[n])
    print(f"[check] Burnside identity matches brute-force orbit enumeration "
          f"for n <= {verify_bruteforce_upto}.")

    # 2. Moment identity N_n = sum_v rho(v) v^n.
    for n in range(max_n + 1):
        moment = sum((rho[v] * Fraction(v) ** n for v in range(degree + 1)), Fraction(0))
        assert moment == burnside[n]
    print("[check] N_n equals the n-th moment of the fixed-point density.")

    # 3. Linear reconstruction from the first |X|+1 orbit counts.
    recovered = reconstruct_density(burnside, degree)
    assert recovered == rho
    print(f"[check] Vandermonde inversion recovers rho from N_0..N_{degree} exactly:")
    print(f"        recovered rho = {[str(r) for r in recovered]}")

    # 4. Peeling recursion with certified rounding.
    peeled, exponents = peel_reconstruct(group, degree)
    assert peeled == counts
    print("[check] peeling recursion recovers the fibre counts exactly:")
    print(f"        peeled F(v)   = {peeled}")
    print(f"        exponent used at each m (index v) = {exponents}")

    # 5. Error bound and monotone convergence of the top peeling step.
    if degree >= 1:
        print(f"        top step: N_n / |X|^n -> |K|/|G| = {rho[degree]}")
        for n in (1, 2, 4, 8, 16):
            approx = Fraction(orbit_count_burnside(group, n)) / Fraction(degree) ** n
            bound = Fraction(degree - 1, degree) ** n if degree >= 1 else Fraction(0)
            err = approx - rho[degree]
            assert 0 <= err <= bound
            print(f"          n = {n:2d}:  P(n) = {float(approx):.10f}   "
                  f"error = {float(err):.3e}   bound = {float(bound):.3e}")


def demo_universal_coefficients() -> None:
    banner("The reconstruction coefficients are universal: they depend only on |X|")
    for size in (2, 3):
        coeff = reconstruction_matrix(size)
        print(f"\nnodes 0..{size}:   rho(v) = sum_n C[v][n] * N_n   with C =")
        for v, row in enumerate(coeff):
            print(f"    v = {v}: " + "  ".join(f"{str(c):>7}" for c in row))
    print("\nFor |X| = 2 this says, for EVERY action on a 2-element set:")
    print("    rho(2) = (N_2 - N_1)/2,   rho(1) = 2N_1 - N_2,   "
          "rho(0) = N_0 - (3/2)N_1 + N_2/2.")


def demo_normalisation_necessary() -> None:
    banner("Sharpness I: normalisation cannot be removed")
    identity2: Perm = (0, 1)
    trivial_group_order_1 = [identity2]
    # A group of order 2 acting trivially: two distinct elements, both acting as identity.
    # We model this by weighting: the fixed-point multiset is {2, 2}, density delta_2.
    print("Trivial group E acting on a 2-element set:")
    print(f"    Phi(q) = {q_series_string(trivial_group_order_1, 2)}"
          f"      orbit counts = {[orbit_count_burnside(trivial_group_order_1, n) for n in range(6)]}")
    print("Order-2 group C_2 acting trivially on the same 2-element set:")
    print("    Phi(q) = 2q^2      orbit counts = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32]")
    print("Both have density rho = delta_2 (all mass at v = 2) and identical orbit")
    print("counts 2^n in every degree; the q-series differ (q^2 versus 2q^2).")
    print("=> orbit counts are blind to |G|: Burnside divides by it.")


def demo_coefficient_bound_sharp() -> None:
    banner("Sharpness II: the number of coefficients cannot be reduced")
    weight = {0: Fraction(1), 1: Fraction(-3), 2: Fraction(3), 3: Fraction(-1)}
    for n in range(4):
        value = sum((weight[v] * Fraction(v) ** n for v in weight), Fraction(0))
        verdict = "vanishes" if value == 0 else f"= {value}  <-- first nonzero"
        print(f"    power sum with exponent n = {n}: {verdict}")
    print("The signed weight (1, -3, 3, -1) on the four nodes {0,1,2,3} kills the")
    print("first three power sums.  So k-1 moments never suffice on k nodes: the")
    print("range n = 0..k-1 in the rigidity theorem is exactly right.")


def demo_group_structure_invisible() -> None:
    banner("Sharpness III: the invariants cannot see the group -- Z/4 versus Z/2 x Z/2")

    # Regular action of Z/4 on itself: generated by the 4-cycle.
    c4 = generated_group([(1, 2, 3, 0)], 4)
    # Regular action of Z/2 x Z/2 on itself: two commuting fixed-point-free involutions.
    v4 = generated_group([(1, 0, 3, 2), (2, 3, 0, 1)], 4)

    for name, group in (("Z/4 (regular)", c4), ("Z/2 x Z/2 (regular)", v4)):
        counts = [orbit_count_burnside(group, n) for n in range(6)]
        print(f"{name:22s} |G| = {len(group)}   "
              f"Phi(q) = {q_series_string(group, 4)}   N_0..N_5 = {counts}")

    same_q = fibre_counts(c4, 4) == fibre_counts(v4, 4)
    same_counts = all(orbit_count_burnside(c4, n) == orbit_count_burnside(v4, n)
                      for n in range(40))
    print(f"\nidentical fixed-point q-series?  {same_q}")
    print(f"identical orbit counts (n < 40)? {same_counts}")
    print("Z/4 is cyclic and Z/2 x Z/2 is not, so the groups are NOT isomorphic.")
    print("=> the rigidity theorem determines the fixed-point distribution and")
    print("   provably nothing more.")


def demo_molien_rational_form() -> None:
    banner("The Molien closed form:  |G| * N(t) = sum_g 1/(1 - |X^g| t)")
    group = generated_group([(1, 0, 2), (0, 2, 1)], 3)      # Sym(3) on 3 points
    order = len(group)
    print(f"Sym(3) on 3 points, |G| = {order}, fixed-point multiset = "
          f"{sorted(fix_count(p) for p in group)}")
    print("\n  n :  |G|*N_n   sum_g |X^g|^n   1/(1-3t)+3/(1-t)+2  coefficient")
    for n in range(7):
        lhs = order * orbit_count_burnside(group, n)
        rhs = sum(fix_count(p) ** n for p in group)
        closed = 3 ** n + 3 * 1 ** n + (2 if n == 0 else 0)
        assert lhs == rhs == closed

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Perm = Tuple[int, ...]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Basic group / action machinery
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def compose(p: Perm, q: Perm) -> Perm:
    """Composition (p after q): (p*q)[i] = p[q[i]]."""
    return tuple(p[q[i]] for i in range(len(p)))


def generated_group(gens: Sequence[Perm], degree: int) -> List[Perm]:
    """Closure of `gens` under composition, containing the identity."""
    identity: Perm = tuple(range(degree))
    elements: Dict[Perm, None] = {identity: None}
    frontier: List[Perm] = [identity]
    while frontier:
        new_frontier: List[Perm] = []
        for element in frontier:
            for g in gens:
                candidate = compose(g, element)
                if candidate not in elements:
                    elements[candidate] = None
                    new_frontier.append(candidate)
        frontier = new_frontier
    return sorted(elements)


def fix_count(p: Perm) -> int:
    """Number of points fixed by the permutation p."""
    return sum(1 for i, image in enumerate(p) if image == i)


def fibre_counts(group: Sequence[Perm], degree: int) -> List[int]:
    """F(v) = #{g in G : |X^g| = v} for v = 0..degree."""
    counts = [0] * (degree + 1)
    for p in group:
        counts[fix_count(p)] += 1
    return counts


def density(group: Sequence[Perm], degree: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    """rho(v) = F(v) / |G| for v = 0..degree."""
    order = len(group)
    return [Fraction(f, order) for f in fibre_counts(group, degree)]


def q_series_string(group: Sequence[Perm], degree: int) -> str:
    """Human-readable fixed-point q-series Phi(q) = sum_g q^{|X^g|}."""
    counts = fibre_counts(group, degree)
    terms: List[str] = []
    for v in range(degree, -1, -1):
        c = counts[v]
        if c == 0:
            continue
        coeff = "" if (c == 1 and v > 0) else str(c)
        if v == 0:
            terms.append(str(c))
        elif v == 1:
            terms.append(f"{coeff}q")
        else:
            terms.append(f"{coeff}q^{v}")
    return " + ".join(terms) if terms else "0"


def orbit_count_bruteforce(group: Sequence[Perm], degree: int, n: int) -> int:
    """#(X^n / G), computed by explicit orbit enumeration (small n only)."""
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    seen = set()
    orbits = 0
    for tup in product(range(degree), repeat=n):
        if tup in seen:
            continue
        orbits += 1
        for p in group:
            seen.add(tuple(p[x] for x in tup))
    return orbits


def orbit_count_burnside(group: Sequence[Perm], n: int) -> int:
    """#(X^n / G) via Burnside: (1/|G|) sum_g |X^g|^n."""
    total = sum(fix_count(p) ** n for p in group)
    assert total % len(group) == 0
    return total // len(group)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Exact linear algebra over Q: Vandermonde inversion
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def moment_matrix(size: int) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    """M[n][j] = j^n for 0 <= n, j <= size (transpose of the Vandermonde matrix)."""
    return [[Fraction(j) ** n for j in range(size + 1)] for n in range(size + 1)]


def invert_matrix(matrix: List[List[Fraction]]) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    """Exact Gauss-Jordan inversion over the rationals."""
    dim = len(matrix)
    work = [row[:] + [Fraction(1 if i == j else 0) for j in range(dim)]
            for i, row in enumerate(matrix)]
    for col in range(dim):
        pivot = next(r for r in range(col, dim) if work[r][col] != 0)
        work[col], work[pivot] = work[pivot], work[col]
        scale = work[col][col]
        work[col] = [entry / scale for entry in work[col]]
        for r in range(dim):
            if r != col and work[r][col] != 0:
                factor = work[r][col]
                work[r] = [a - factor * b for a, b in zip(work[r], work[col])]
    return [row[dim:] for row in work]


def reconstruction_matrix(size: int) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    """C = M^{-1}: the universal reconstruction coefficients on nodes 0..size."""
    return invert_matrix(moment_matrix(size))


def reconstruct_density(orbit_counts: Sequence[int], size: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    """rho(v) = sum_{n<=size} C[v][n] * N_n, using exactly size+1 orbit counts."""
    coeff = reconstruction_matrix(size)
    return [sum((coeff[v][n] * orbit_counts[n] for n in range(size + 1)), Fraction(0))
            for v in range(size + 1)]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The peeling recursion, with certified rounding
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def peel_estimate(orbit_counts_at_n: Fraction, known_above: Sequence[Fraction],
                  m: int, size: int, n: int) -> Fraction:
    """P_m(n) = (N_n - sum_{v>m} rho(v) v^n) / m^n, with known_above indexed by v."""
    tail = sum((known_above[v] * Fraction(v) ** n for v in range(m + 1, size + 1)),
               Fraction(0))
    return (orbit_counts_at_n - tail) / Fraction(m) ** n


def peel_stopping_time(m: int, group_order: int) -> int:
    """Least n with ((m-1)/m)^n * 2|G| < 1 (n = 1 when m = 1, where the error is 0)."""
    if m == 1:
        return 1
    ratio = Fraction(m - 1, m)
    n = 1
    while ratio ** n * 2 * group_order >= 1:
        n += 1
    return n


def round_half_up(x: Fraction) -> int:
    """Nearest integer to the rational x."""
    from math import floor
    return floor(x + Fraction(1, 2))


def peel_reconstruct(group: Sequence[Perm], size: int) -> Tuple[List[int], List[int]]:
    """
    Reconstruct the fibre counts F(0..size) purely from orbit counts, top down.

    Returns (fibre counts, the exponent n used at each value m).
    Uses only |G| and an oracle for the orbit counts; never inspects the group's
    fixed-point data directly.
    """
    order = len(group)
    rho: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(0)] * (size + 1)
    fibres: List[int] = [0] * (size + 1)
    exponents: List[int] = [0] * (size + 1)
    for m in range(size, 0, -1):
        n = peel_stopping_time(m, order)
        exponents[m] = n
        n_at = Fraction(orbit_count_burnside(group, n))
        estimate = peel_estimate(n_at, rho, m, size, n)
        fibres[m] = round_half_up(Fraction(order) * estimate)
        rho[m] = Fraction(fibres[m], order)
    fibres[0] = order - sum(fibres[1:])
    return fibres, exponents

# 4. Demonstrations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

def banner(text: str) -> None:

    banner(f"{name}   (|G| = {len(group)}, |X| = {degree})")

    counts = fibre_counts(group, degree)
    rho = density(group, degree)
    print(f"fixed-point q-series  Phi(q) = {q_series_string(group, degree)}")
    print(f"fibre counts F(v)            = {counts}")
    print(f"density rho(v)               = {[str(r) for r in rho]}")
    print(f"total mass                   = {sum(rho, Fraction(0))}")

    burnside = [orbit_count_burnside(group, n) for n in range(max_n + 1)]
    print(f"orbit counts N_0..N_{max_n}        = {burnside}")

    for n in range(verify_bruteforce_upto + 1):

    for n in range(max_n + 1):

        assert moment == burnside[n]
    print("[check] N_n equals the n-th moment of the fixed-point density.")

    # 3. Linear reconstruction from the first |X|+1 orbit counts.
    recovered = reconstruct_density(burnside, degree)

    print(f"[check] Vandermonde inversion recovers rho from N_0..N_{degree} exactly:")
    print(f"        recovered rho = {[str(r) for r in recovered]}")

    print(f"        peeled F(v)   = {peeled}")

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import combinations, permutations
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Perm = Tuple[int, ...]


def compose(p: Perm, q: Perm) -> Perm:
    return tuple(p[q[i]] for i in range(len(p)))


def closure(gens: Sequence[Perm], degree: int) -> Tuple[Perm, ...]:
    identity: Perm = tuple(range(degree))
    seen = {identity}
    frontier = [identity]
    while frontier:
        nxt: List[Perm] = []
        for element in frontier:
            for g in gens:
                cand = compose(g, element)
                if cand not in seen:
                    seen.add(cand)
                    nxt.append(cand)
        frontier = nxt
    return tuple(sorted(seen))


def all_subgroups(degree: int) -> List[Tuple[Perm, ...]]:
    """All subgroups of Sym(degree), found by closing every set of <= 2 generators."""
    elements = list(permutations(range(degree)))
    found: Dict[Tuple[Perm, ...], None] = {}
    for g in elements:
        found[closure([g], degree)] = None
    for g, h in combinations(elements, 2):
        found[closure([g, h], degree)] = None
    return sorted(found, key=lambda grp: (len(grp), grp))


def fibres(group: Sequence[Perm], degree: int) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    counts = [0] * (degree + 1)
    for p in group:
        counts[sum(1 for i, im in enumerate(p) if im == i)] += 1
    return tuple(counts)


def orbit_counts(group: Sequence[Perm], degree: int, upto: int) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    order = len(group)
    fib = fibres(group, degree)
    return tuple(sum(f * v ** n for v, f in enumerate(fib)) // order
                 for n in range(upto + 1))


def density(group: Sequence[Perm], degree: int) -> Tuple[Fraction, ...]:
    order = len(group)
    return tuple(Fraction(f, order) for f in fibres(group, degree))


def main() -> None:
    degree = 4
    groups = all_subgroups(degree)
    print(f"All subgroups of Sym({degree}) found by 2-generator closure: {len(groups)}")

    window = degree            # the theorem's window: n <= max(|X|,|Y|)
    horizon = 25               # far beyond the window, to look for late divergence

    late_divergence = 0
    checked = 0
    classes: Dict[Tuple[Fraction, ...], List[Tuple[Perm, ...]]] = {}

    for group in groups:
        classes.setdefault(density(group, degree), []).append(group)

    for a, b in combinations(groups, 2):
        short_a = orbit_counts(a, degree, window)
        short_b = orbit_counts(b, degree, window)
        if short_a != short_b:
            continue
        checked += 1
        long_a = orbit_counts(a, degree, horizon)
        long_b = orbit_counts(b, degree, horizon)
        if long_a != long_b:
            late_divergence += 1
        # the theorem also predicts equal densities
        assert density(a, degree) == density(b, degree)

    print(f"of those, pairs that later diverge (n <= {horizon}): {late_divergence}")
    print("(the dichotomy predicts 0)")

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple


def moment_matrix(size: int) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    """M[n][j] = j^n, 0 <= n, j <= size: the transpose of the Vandermonde matrix."""
    return [[Fraction(j) ** n for j in range(size + 1)] for n in range(size + 1)]


def invert_matrix(matrix: List[List[Fraction]]) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    """Exact Gauss-Jordan inversion over Q.  O(d^3) rational operations."""
    dim = len(matrix)
    work: List[List[Fraction]] = [
        row[:] + [Fraction(1 if i == j else 0) for j in range(dim)]
        for i, row in enumerate(matrix)
    ]
    for col in range(dim):
        pivot = next(r for r in range(col, dim) if work[r][col] != 0)
        work[col], work[pivot] = work[pivot], work[col]
        scale = work[col][col]
        work[col] = [entry / scale for entry in work[col]]
        for r in range(dim):
            if r != col and work[r][col] != 0:
                factor = work[r][col]
                work[r] = [a - factor * b for a, b in zip(work[r], work[col])]
    return [row[dim:] for row in work]


def reconstruction_matrix(size: int) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    """C = M^{-1}: universal reconstruction coefficients on the nodes 0..size."""
    return invert_matrix(moment_matrix(size))

def stopping_time(m: int, group_order: int) -> int:
    """Least n with ((m-1)/m)^n * 2|G| < 1.  For m = 1 the error is 0^n, so n = 1."""
    if m <= 1:

    ratio = Fraction(m - 1, m)
    n = 1
    while ratio ** n * 2 * group_order >= 1:

    return n


def peel_estimate(orbit_count_at_n: int, known: List[Fraction], m: int,
                  size: int, n: int) -> Fraction:

    tail = sum((known[v] * Fraction(v) ** n for v in range(m + 1, size + 1)),
               Fraction(0))
    return (Fraction(orbit_count_at_n) - tail) / Fraction(m) ** n


def error_bound(m: int, n: int) -> Fraction:
    """The certified bound |P_m(n) - rho(m)| <= ((m-1)/m)^n."""
    return Fraction(max(m - 1, 0), max(m, 1)) ** n

                     group_order: int) -> Tuple[List[int], List[int]]:

    rho: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(0)] * (size + 1)
    fibres: List[int] = [0] * (size + 1)
    exponents: List[int] = [0] * (size + 1)
    for m in range(size, 0, -1):

        rho[m] = Fraction(fibres[m], group_order)
    fibres[0] = group_order - sum(fibres[1:])   # total mass is 1

<h1>The Molien Reconstruction Laboratory</h1>
<p class="lede">
A finite group acting on a finite set casts two shadows: how its elements are distributed by
number of fixed points, and how many orbits it has on tuples. Burnside's lemma says the second
is the sequence of <em>moments</em> of the first. Here you can hide the group, look only at the
orbit counts, and rebuild the fixed-point distribution — exactly.
</p>

<h2>1  ·  The two shadows</h2>

<details>
<summary>Why is the orbit count a moment? (click to expand)</summary>
<p>
Burnside's lemma says that for a finite group acting on a finite set <em>Z</em>, the number of
orbits is the average number of fixed points: |G|·|Z/G| = Σ<sub>g</sub>|Z<sup>g</sup>|. Apply
this not to <em>X</em> but to the set of <em>n</em>-tuples, with the group acting on all
coordinates at once. An element fixes a tuple exactly when it fixes every entry, so the tuples
fixed by <em>g</em> are precisely the tuples drawn from X<sup>g</sup>, of which there are
|X<sup>g</sup>|<sup>n</sup>. Hence |G|·N<sub>n</sub> = Σ<sub>g</sub>|X<sup>g</sup>|<sup>n</sup>.
Sorting the group elements by their fixed-point count and dividing by |G| turns this into
N<sub>n</sub> = Σ<sub>v</sub> ρ(v)·v<sup>n</sup>: the <em>n</em>-th moment of a probability
measure supported on the grid {0, 1, …, |X|}. Setting n = 0 gives Σ<sub>v</sub>ρ(v) = 1.
</p>
</details>

<h2>2  ·  Reconstruction by inverting the moment matrix</h2>
<div class="card">
  <p class="note" style="margin-top:0">
    The moment matrix on the nodes 0,1,…,N has entries M<sub>n,j</sub> = j<sup>n</sup>: it is the
    transpose of the Vandermonde matrix, hence invertible. Its inverse C is a universal array of
    rational numbers depending on <strong>N = |X| alone</strong> — not on the group, not on the
    action, not even on |G|. One matrix–vector product turns the first N+1 orbit counts into the
    whole density.
  </p>

  </div>
</div>

<details>
<summary>Why exactly N+1 coefficients, and why not fewer?</summary>
<p>
Both densities live on the same N+1 nodes. If two of them had the same first N+1 moments, their
difference <em>w</em> would be a signed weight on N+1 nodes with N+1 vanishing power sums. Fix a
node <em>u</em> and let L<sub>u</sub> be the Lagrange basis polynomial that is 1 at <em>u</em> and
0 at the other nodes; it has degree ≤ N, so expanding it in powers writes
w(u) = Σ<sub>v</sub> w(v)L<sub>u</sub>(v) as a combination of the vanishing power sums. Hence
w(u) = 0 for every u.
</p>
<p>
One coefficient fewer is genuinely not enough: on the four nodes {0,1,2,3} the signed weight
(1, −3, 3, −1) — the third finite-difference functional — kills the power sums for n = 0, 1, 2
and gives −6 at n = 3. So the window n ≤ |X| is exactly the right size.
</p>
</details>

<details>
<summary>What can these invariants never see?</summary>
<p>
Two things, and exactly two. First, the <strong>group order</strong>: Burnside divides by |G|, so
inflating a group while it acts through the same quotient leaves every orbit count unchanged. The
trivial group and the group of order two, both acting trivially on a two-element set, have
identical orbit counts 2<sup>n</sup> but q-series q² and 2q².
</p>
<p>
Second, the <strong>group itself</strong>. When a group acts on itself by translation, the
identity fixes everything and nothing else fixes anything, so both invariants depend on |G| alone.
The cyclic group of order 4 and the Klein four-group therefore have identical fixed-point
q-series q⁴+3 and identical orbit counts 1, 1, 4, 16, 64, … in every degree, although one is
cyclic and the other is not. The reconstruction theorem recovers the fixed-point distribution and
provably nothing finer.
</p>
</details>

Suppose someone hands you a counting machine. For each $n$ it tells you how many *essentially
different* strings of length $n$ there are, where "essentially different" means "not related by
one of the symmetries in a hidden group $G$ acting on the alphabet $X$". You never see the group.
You see only the numbers

$$N_0,\; N_1,\; N_2,\; N_3,\; \dots$$

**How much of the hidden symmetry can you reconstruct?** By the end of this page you will know
the complete answer: exactly one probability distribution, recoverable from finitely many counts,
by an algorithm that provably terminates — and nothing else, ever.

---

## 1. Two shadows of one action

Let $G$ be a finite group acting on a finite set $X$. Write $X^g = \{x : g\cdot x = x\}$ for the
points that $g$ leaves alone. Two objects record the action's behaviour.

**The fixed-point $q$-series** collects the group elements by how much they fix:
$$\Phi(q) = \sum_{g \in G} q^{\,|X^g|}.$$
Normalising, we get a probability distribution on $\{0,1,\dots,|X|\}$:
$$\rho(v) = \frac{\#\{g \in G : |X^g| = v\}}{|G|}.$$

**The orbit-counting sequence** records how many orbits the group has on $n$-tuples:
$$N_n = \bigl|\, X^{\times n}/G \,\bigr|.$$

These look like completely different animals. Burnside's lemma, applied not to $X$ but to the set
of $n$-tuples, says they are two views of one thing:

$$\boxed{\;N_n \;=\; \sum_{v=0}^{|X|} \rho(v)\, v^{\,n}\;}$$

The orbit counts are the **moments** of the fixed-point distribution. That single sentence is the
whole subject.

<details>
<summary>Click for the derivation of the moment identity</summary>

Burnside's lemma: for a finite group acting on a finite set $Z$, the number of orbits equals the
average number of fixed points, $|G|\cdot|Z/G| = \sum_g |Z^g|$. Apply this with $Z = X^{\times n}$
and the coordinatewise action. An element $g$ fixes a tuple exactly when it fixes every entry, so
the tuples fixed by $g$ are precisely the tuples drawn from $X^g$, of which there are $|X^g|^n$.
Therefore
$$|G| \cdot N_n = \sum_{g \in G} |X^g|^{\,n}.$$
Sorting the group elements by their fixed-point count and dividing by $|G|$ gives the boxed
identity. Setting $n = 0$ shows $N_0 = 1$ and $\sum_v \rho(v) = 1$: the density really is a
probability measure. Read more about [Burnside's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnside%27s_lemma)
and its enumerative descendant, [Pólya's theory of counting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%B3lya_enumeration_theorem).
</details>

Summing the geometric series term by term gives a closed form of *Molien type*:
$$|G| \cdot \sum_{n\ge0} N_n t^n \;=\; \sum_{g\in G} \frac{1}{1 - |X^g|\,t},$$
so the counting series is a rational function whose poles are the reciprocals of the fixed-point
counts and whose residues are proportional to how many elements realise each count. Reconstruction
will amount to *hearing the poles and residues from finitely many Taylor coefficients*.

---

## 3. Why finitely many counts suffice

Here is the rigidity theorem, in full.

> **Theorem (rigidity and dichotomy).** Let $G$ act on $X$ and $H$ on $Y$. If the orbit counts
> agree for every $n \le \max(|X|,|Y|)$, then the normalised fixed-point distributions are
> identical. Conversely, equal distributions give equal counts in every degree. Consequently, for
> groups of the *same order*, either the fixed-point $q$-series coincide, or the orbit-counting
> sequences already differ at some $n \le \max(|X|,|Y|)$ — there is no middle ground.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the proof (it is Lagrange interpolation, not group theory)</summary>

Both distributions are supported on the same node set $S = \{0,1,\dots,\max(|X|,|Y|)\}$, of size
$k = |S|$. Let $w(v)$ be the difference of the two densities. The hypothesis says
$$\sum_{v \in S} w(v)\,v^{\,n} = 0 \qquad \text{for } n = 0, 1, \dots, k-1.$$
Fix a node $u$ and let
$$L_u(T) = \prod_{v \ne u} \frac{T - v}{u - v}$$
be the [Lagrange basis polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_polynomial): it equals
$1$ at $u$ and $0$ at every other node, and has degree $k-1$. Then
$$w(u) = \sum_{v \in S} w(v)\,L_u(v) = \sum_{n<k} c_n \sum_{v \in S} w(v)\,v^{\,n} = 0,$$
where $c_n$ are the coefficients of $L_u$. So $w \equiv 0$.

The whole content is: *$k$ vanishing power sums on $k$ distinct nodes force the weights to
vanish.* Everything else in the theory is bookkeeping around this one fact.
</details>

Could fewer coefficients do? No. On the four nodes $\{0,1,2,3\}$ the signed vector
$(1,-3,3,-1)$ — the third finite-difference functional — annihilates the power sums for
$n = 0,1,2$ and gives $-6$ at $n=3$. Three moments cannot see a difference spread over four
nodes. The window $n \le |X|$ is exactly the right size.

---

## 4. Reconstruction, method one: one universal matrix

Uniqueness is not an algorithm. Here is the algorithm.

Build the *moment matrix* $M$ on the nodes $0,1,\dots,N$, with $M_{n,j} = j^{\,n}$. It is the
transpose of the [Vandermonde matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandermonde_matrix), so it is
invertible. Let $C = M^{-1}$.

> **Theorem (linear reconstruction).** For every $v \le N = |X|$,
> $$\rho(v) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} C_{v,n}\, N_n.$$
> The matrix $C$ depends only on $N$ — not on the group, not on the action, not even on $|G|$.

For $N = 2$, for instance,
$$C = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -\tfrac32 & \tfrac12\\ 0 & 2 & -1\\ 0 & -\tfrac12 & \tfrac12\end{pmatrix},$$
so for **every** action on a two-element set, $\rho(2) = \tfrac12(N_2 - N_1)$: the fraction of the
group acting trivially is half the gap between the second and first orbit counts.

{{algorithm:0}}

---

## 5. Reconstruction, method two: peel from the top

The second method is slower in the number of counts it consumes but far more revealing — and much
better behaved numerically, since Vandermonde inversion is famously ill-conditioned.

Suppose you already know the densities above some level $m$. Subtract their contributions from the
$n$-th orbit count and divide by $m^n$:
$$P_m(n) = \frac{N_n - \sum_{v>m}\rho(v)v^{\,n}}{m^{\,n}} = \sum_{v \le m} \rho(v)\left(\frac vm\right)^{\!n}.$$
Every term with $v<m$ decays geometrically, so $P_m(n) \to \rho(m)$. Work downward from
$m = |X|$; close with $\rho(0) = 1 - \sum_{v\ge1}\rho(v)$, forced by total mass.

The top step deserves its own name. Taking $m = |X|$ (nothing to subtract),
$$\frac{N_n}{|X|^{\,n}} \longrightarrow \frac{|K|}{|G|},$$
where $K$ is the kernel of the action. The growth rate of the orbit count is $|X|$, and its
leading constant is the proportion of the group that acts trivially.

{{visualization:0}}

<details>
<summary>Why the limit is a finite computation, not just a limit</summary>

Two facts combine. First, the error is explicitly geometric: since the densities are nonnegative
with total mass at most $1$ below $m$,
$$0 \;\le\; P_m(n) - \rho(m) \;\le\; \left(\frac{m-1}{m}\right)^{\! n}.$$
Second, the answer has bounded denominator: $\rho(m) = \#\{g : |X^g| = m\}/|G|$. A rational with
known denominator is pinned down by any approximation good to within half a unit after scaling.
Hence as soon as
$$\left(\frac{m-1}{m}\right)^{\! n}\cdot 2|G| < 1,$$
the integer nearest to $|G|\cdot P_m(n)$ is *exactly* $\#\{g : |X^g| = m\}$. Such an $n$ always
exists because $(m-1)/m < 1$; it grows like $m\log(2|G|)$. The asymptotic statement has become a
terminating algorithm with a stopping rule.

This pattern — geometric approximation, plus a denominator bound, plus rounding — is a general
recipe for turning limits into exact computations in arithmetic settings.
</details>

{{algorithm:1}}

Underneath both methods sits the orbit-count oracle itself, which is where Burnside earns its
keep: computing $N_n$ by enumerating $|X|^n$ tuples is hopeless, while the moment formula makes
each count cost a handful of integer operations.

{{algorithm:2}}

## 7. What is lost — and it is exactly two things

Rigidity theorems earn their keep at the edges. This one has two, and both are theorems rather
than gaps in an argument.

**The group order is invisible.** Burnside divides by $|G|$, so inflating the group while it acts
through the same quotient leaves every orbit count unchanged. The trivial group and the group of
order two, each acting trivially on a two-element set, both give $N_n = 2^n$, but their $q$-series
are $q^2$ and $2q^2$. This is why the correct converse invariant is the normalised distribution
$\rho$ and not the raw series $\Phi$.

**The group itself is invisible.** When a group acts on itself by translation, the identity fixes
everything and nothing else fixes anything, so
$$\Phi(q) = q^{|G|} + (|G| - 1), \qquad N_{n+1} = |G|^{\,n}$$
depend on $|G|$ alone. Hence the cyclic group of order $4$ and the Klein four-group, acting on
themselves, have identical $q$-series $q^4+3$ and identical orbit counts $1,1,4,16,64,\dots$ in
every degree — while one is cyclic and the other is not. The theorem determines the fixed-point
distribution and can never be upgraded to determine the group.

The mirror image is clean: if you know in advance that both actions come from *the same* group,
the normalisation ambiguity evaporates and rigidity upgrades from densities to raw counts —
agreement of the first $\max(|X|,|Y|)+1$ orbit counts becomes *equivalent* to equality of the
multisets $\{|X^g|\}$ and $\{|Y^g|\}$.

The search below tests the dichotomy exhaustively over all subgroups of the symmetric group on
four points, and finds no late divergence anywhere — as predicted.

## 8. Where this sits

Three threads meet here.

* **Enumerative combinatorics.** [Pólya theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%B3lya_enumeration_theorem)
  runs forwards, from a symmetry group to a counting series. This is the inverse problem, and the
  inverse map is explicit.
* **The moment problem.** The counting series is the moment sequence of a probability measure on a
  finite grid; uniqueness from finitely many moments is classical, but the *bounded denominator*
  is special to this setting, and it is what makes the reconstruction exact and finite.
* **Invariant theory.** The shape $\sum_g (1-|X^g|t)^{-1}$ is a combinatorial echo of
  [Molien's series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molien_series) for rings of invariants, and the
  whole story runs gradewise for graded families of finite sets.

Strip everything away and the picture is simple. A group action casts two shadows; one is the
moment sequence of the other; moments determine a measure on a finite grid; and the arithmetic of
the measure makes the determination effective. What survives the shadow-casting is a probability
distribution. What is lost is a scale and a structure. There is no room left for anything else.

section Algebra

/-- **Finite determinacy of weighted power sums.**  If the weighted power sums
